title: Sildenafil
description: Drug for erectile dysfunction and hypertension
wiki_lead:
Sildenafil, sold under the brand name Viagra among others, is a medication used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension. It is also sometimes used off-label for the treatment of certain symptoms in secondary Raynaud's phenomenon. It is unclear if it is effective for treating sexual dysfunction in females. It can be taken orally (swallowed by mouth), intravenously (injection into a vein), or through the sublingual route (dissolved under the tongue). Onset when taken orally is typically within twenty minutes and lasts for about two hours.
Common side effects include headaches, heartburn, and flushed skin. Caution is advised in those with cardiovascular disease. Rare but serious side effects include vision problems, hearing loss, and prolonged erection (priapism) that can lead to damage to the penis. Sildenafil should not be taken by people on nitric oxide donors such as nitroglycerin, as this may result in a serious drop in blood pressure.
Sildenafil acts by blocking phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5), an enzyme that promotes breakdown of cGMP, which regulates blood flow in the penis. It requires sexual arousal to work, and does not by itself cause or increase sexual arousal. It also results in dilation of the blood vessels in the lungs.
Pfizer originally discovered the medication in 1989 while looking for a treatment for angina. It was approved for medical use in the United States and in the European Union in 1998. In 2023, it was the 151st most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 3 million prescriptions. It is available as a generic medication. In the United Kingdom, it is available as a pharmacy medicine.

Medical uses


Erectile dysfunction
The primary indication of sildenafil is treatment of erectile dysfunction (inability to sustain a satisfactory erection to complete sexual intercourse). Its use is now one of the standard treatments for erectile dysfunction, including for males with diabetes mellitus.
Tentative evidence suggests that sildenafil may help males who experience antidepressant-induced erectile dysfunction.


Pulmonary hypertension
While sildenafil improves some markers of disease in people with pulmonary arterial hypertension, it does not appear to affect the risk of death or serious side effects.


Raynaud's phenomenon
Sildenafil and other PDE5 inhibitors are used off-label to alleviate vasospasm and treat severe ischemia and ulcers in fingers and toes for people with secondary Raynaud's phenomenon; these drugs have moderate efficacy for reducing the frequency and duration of vasospastic episodes. As of 2016, their role more generally in Raynaud's was not clear.


Altitude sickness
Sildenafil has shown some potential for improving exercise performance at high altitudes. However, its overall efficacy is not clear. 


High-altitude pulmonary edema
Sildenafil has been studied for high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), but its use is currently not recommended for that indication.

Sildenafil (Korean: ì¤ë°ëí) is a selective phosphodiesterase type 5 ( PDE5) inhibitor medication primarily used to treat erectile dysfunction (ED) in men and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) in adults and children. Sildenafil (Viagra) is not considered a narcotic drug and is not included in narcotic substance lists in Russia or most other countries. It is available as a prescription medication in most jurisdictions, but over-the-counter without a prescription in select European countries, including the United Kingdom (as Viagra Connect since 2018), Ireland (since 2021), Poland (since 2016), Norway (since 2020), and Portugal (sildenafil 50 mg since May 2025, exclusively dispensed in pharmacies following an Infarmed protocol). Unlike substances with high abuse potential such as opioids and cocaine. Originally developed in the 1980s by Pfizer as a potential treatment for angina and hypertension, its unexpected side effect of inducing erections during clinical trials led to its repurposing and FDA approval in 1998 under the brand name Viagra for ED, marking a revolutionary advancement in sexual medicine. Sildenafil works by inhibiting the PDE5 enzyme, which normally breaks down cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP); this inhibition promotes smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation in the corpus cavernosum of the penis during sexual stimulation for ED, or in the pulmonary vasculature to reduce blood pressure for PAH. Contrary to a common misconception, the idea that sildenafil causes spontaneous erections without sexual stimulation is a myth; sildenafil has no effect in the absence of sexual stimulation and enhances the body's natural response to sexual arousal but requires such arousal or stimulation to produce an erection. Anecdotal reports of perceived spontaneous erections are generally attributed to subconscious arousal or minimal stimulation, aligning with the medical consensus. Sexual stimulation sufficient to enable sildenafil's effects can arise from mental imagination or fantasy alone (including during masturbation). Sildenafil does not enhance sexual imagination, fantasy, desire, or libido and does not alter mental aspects of sexuality; it solely facilitates penile blood flow in response to preexisting arousal, which may help produce stronger erections in individuals with erectile difficulties. 

Another widespread misconception involves "Viagra before and after pictures" or similar online images claiming to show dramatic physical transformations, such as permanent increases in penis size or visible anatomical changes. Sildenafil does not alter the penis's structure or size permanently; it temporarily improves blood flow to support firmer erections during sexual stimulation. Any purported "before and after" photos depicting visible changes are typically misleading, edited, fabricated, or unrelated to the medication's actual effects, which are functional rather than cosmetic. Clinical trials and medical sources confirm that benefits are in erectile performance (e.g., successful intercourse rates of approximately 60-70% in treated groups versus 20-30% with placebo in key studies), not permanent physical modifications. Patients seeking visual proof should rely on evidence-based information rather than anecdotal or marketed images.

Sildenafil requires sexual arousal or stimulation to be effective for erectile dysfunction and does not cure the underlying condition. It also does not protect against sexually transmitted infections. It is available in oral tablet form (recommended starting dose of 50 mg for ED, taken as needed approximately 1 hour before sexual activity, adjustable to 25 mg or 100 mg based on efficacy and tolerability; dosage is not weight-based, and no specific adjustments are recommended for obesity, body weight, or BMI, with efficacy independent of BMI) and as Revatio for PAH (20 mg three times daily), with formulations also including oral suspensions and injectables for specific indications. Off-label applications include conditions like Raynaud's phenomenon and high-altitude pulmonary edema, though these are not FDA-approved. Emerging research, including recent observational studies and reviews, suggests that sildenafil and other PDE5 inhibitors may offer potential non-sexual health benefits, such as reduced risk of stroke, improved cardiovascular outcomes, possible protection against Alzheimer's disease, and associations with increased longevity; however, these findings are preliminary, derived primarily from observational data, and are not yet established as approved indications, requiring confirmation through randomized controlled trials. Since its introduction, sildenafil has significantly improved quality of life for millions, with high efficacy rates (up to 80% success in ED treatment) and a favorable safety profile when used appropriately; however, it is contraindicated with nitrates due to the risk of severe hypotension and requires caution in patients with cardiovascular disease, particularly when coadministered with antihypertensive medications such as amlodipine due to the potential for additive hypotensive effects. Common adverse effects, which are generally mild to moderate and of short duration, include headache, facial flushing, dyspepsia (indigestion), nasal congestion, visual disorders (such as color distortion or blurred vision), dizziness, nausea, and hot flushes, while rare serious events include priapism, sudden vision or hearing loss, non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), cardiovascular events (such as myocardial infarction or arrhythmia), and severe skin reactions (such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis). Patients experiencing serious symptoms should seek immediate medical attention. By 2005, it had also been approved for PAH, expanding its therapeutic scope beyond sexual health.
